## The idea

A familiar tune can sometimes survive being tapped on a single pitch. In that
case rhythm is carrying more of its identity than the note names. Give every
note the same duration and a different part of the tune may survive through its
rise and fall. Because an ordinary melody combines these streams, listening to
the finished line does not always reveal which one made it recognisable.

*Contour* is a reduced description of pitch motion: up, down, or unchanged. It
forgets interval size and absolute register. Rhythm can be separated into onset
and duration data. Once the streams live in independent arrays, you can make a
clean comparison: flatten all pitches while preserving time, replace the timing
while preserving shape, or change every interval size without changing its
direction.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 104
use_synth :pluck

notes = [64, 64, 66, 64, 69, 68, 64, 64, 66, 64, 71, 69]
durations = [0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 2, 0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 2]

define :play_phrase do |notes, durations|
  notes.zip(durations).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.75
    sleep duration
  end
end

define :contour do |notes|
  notes.each_cons(2).map do |a, b|
    b > a ? :up : (b < a ? :down : :same)
  end
end

shape = contour(notes)
contour_notes = [60]
shape.each do |direction|
  step = {up: 2, down: -2, same: 0}[direction]
  contour_notes << contour_notes[-1] + step
end

play_phrase notes, durations
sleep 2
play_phrase Array.new(notes.length, 64), durations
sleep 2
play_phrase contour_notes, Array.new(notes.length, 0.75)
sleep 2
play_phrase contour_notes, durations
```

The first pass presents the complete phrase. The second keeps its rhythm and
removes pitch motion, so any remaining identity belongs largely to timing. The
third rebuilds only the coarse contour on equal durations. The fourth restores
the original rhythm to that rebuilt shape. Listen across the sequence for what
disappears at each reduction and what returns when the two streams meet again.

## Change one thing

1. Replace every duration with `1`. The original pitches remain, but their
   distinctive long and short values disappear. Notice which fragments still
   sound connected and where the phrase loses its former boundaries.
2. Change the rebuilt contour step from two semitones to one. Every direction
   stays fixed while the line contracts into half the pitch range. This tests
   how much interval size contributed beyond the signs of the motion.
3. Reverse only `durations`. The notes keep their order, but long values now
   emphasise different pitches. Listen for a new grouping rather than expecting
   a backward version of the original tune.

## Why it works

`zip` aligns the note and duration streams by index, and `play_phrase` combines
them only at playback. A timing experiment therefore need not rewrite pitch
data, while a pitch transformation leaves rhythm intact. The architecture makes
the listening comparison as local as the code change.

Contour is deliberately lossy. Many different melodies reduce to the same
sequence of directions, which makes family resemblance visible but prevents
reconstruction of the source. A duration list is incomplete too once meter,
accent, and articulation enter. The examples ask a narrower, answerable question:
given these reductions of this phrase, which preserved feature carries more of
what you recognise?

The answer varies with both melody and listener. Rhythm often carries a striking
amount of identity, but that observation should be tested with another person
rather than promoted to a universal rule. The uncertainty is useful in later
transcription work. A secure rhythmic outline with approximate pitches may lead
you to the phrase sooner than exact notes floating at uncertain times.

You can enrich contour in stages. Replace `:up` with categories such as
`:step_up` and `:leap_up`, or store the complete signed semitone difference.
Every added distinction retains more identity and allows fewer source melodies
to share the encoding. Use the coarsest representation that answers the current
question; add detail when two musically relevant cases still collapse together.

## Take it further

Choose a familiar tune of eight to sixteen notes and make three anonymous
versions: its original rhythm on one pitch, its contour with equal durations,
and its original rhythm paired with contour rebuilt in whole tones. Play them
for a willing listener and record which version they identify first. Hold synth,
tempo, register, and amplitude fixed, and preserve the exact arrays alongside
the observation. That record makes the result reproducible without pretending
one listener settles the general question.
